307: [sec1.p1.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 1 Individual differences in the perception of abiotic individuals: The case of gummy bears Natalie Förster1, Ella Back2, Ada M. Förster2, and Mitja D. Back3 1University of Wuppertal, Institute for Educational Research, Germany 2 independent researcher 3University of Münster, Department of Psychology, Germany Preprint, 29 August 2026.
308: [sec1.p1.s2] Not peer reviewed.
309: [sec1.p1.s3] Please cite as Förster, N., Back, E., Förster, A. M., & Back, M. D. (2026).
310: [sec1.p1.s4] Individual differences in the perception of abiotic individuals: The case of gummy bears.
311: [sec1.p1.s5] Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22163292
312: 
313: [sec1.p2.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 2 Abstract People routinely perceive and evaluate things that are not alive, yet research on those perceptions and evaluations has focused on the level of the category (e.g., perceiving flowers, wine, food, artwork).
314: [sec1.p2.s2] Here we translate research on interpersonal perception to abiotic individuals and investigate individual differences between human perceivers in the accurate perception of and their unique preferences for gummy bear individuals of different flavors.
315: [sec1.p2.s3] Four members of one family, aged 8 to 47, each tasted 25 gummy bears drawn blind (100 trials in total).
316: [sec1.p2.s4] On each trial, the participant named the flavor among six known alternatives (strawberry, orange, apple, raspberry, lemon, pineapple), rated their certainty, and indicated their liking for the gummy bear.
317: [sec1.p2.s5] Liking for each flavor had also been stated before the tasting trials.
318: [sec1.p2.s6] Average accuracy in gummy bear identification (42%) was well above chance level (16.7%), with large interindividual variability (individual accuracies ranged from 12% to 68%).
319: [sec1.p2.s7] While stated liking was largely consensual between the family members, tasted liking was driven by the unique perceiver x flavor pairing.
320: [sec1.p2.s8] Also, stated preferences did not track tasted ones on average, and the correspondence varied widely across the four perceivers.
321: [sec1.p2.s9] Results underline the existence of individual differences in accurate perceptions of and unique preferences for gummy bears and point to fruitful avenues for future research on the perception of abiotic individuals in general.
322: [sec1.p2.s10] Keywords: interpersonal perception, individual differences, flavor identification, accuracy, uniqueness, gummy bears
323: 
324: [sec1.p3.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 3 Statement of Relevance People spend a great deal of their lives evaluating things that are not people: foods, products, objects, media.
325: [sec1.p3.s2] Psychology usually measures these evaluations at the level of the category, by asking which flavors, brands, or designs a person prefers.
326: [sec1.p3.s3] We measured what happens one level down, when a person meets a single member of a category without knowing which category it belongs to, in this case a gummy bear of unknown flavor placed directly in the mouth.
327: [sec1.p3.s4] What our participants said about the flavors in advance agreed well across family members, but the two flavors they named as best beforehand were not the two they liked best in the mouth.
328: [sec1.p3.s5] How well they could identify what they were eating also differed sharply from person to person.
329: [sec1.p3.s6] Two of the four could name the gummy bear flavor in their mouth far more often than guessing would allow, and two were found to be bad gummy bear judges.
330: [sec1.p3.s7] Surveys, menus, gift choices, and reward schemes for children all assume that a stated preference for a category describes the experience of its members.
331: [sec1.p3.s8] Measuring that experience directly is feasible, and it gives a different answer.
332: 
333: [sec1.p4.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 4 Introduction "I only like the red ones!
334: [sec1.p4.s2] (Anonymous, 8 years) People form perceptions of things that are not alive as readily as they form perceptions of one another.
335: [sec1.p4.s3] Processes similar to those that characterize perceptions between humans can not only be found for human perceptions of animals (Gosling et al., 2003), but they also run across perceptions of machines and other objects, stopping at no clear boundary (Epley et al., 2007; Gray et al., 2007).
336: [sec1.p4.s4] The degree to which human-like perceptions are applied to objects varies across human perceivers (Waytz et al., 2010) with consequences for how much individuals are attached to these objects (Chandler & Schwarz, 2010).
337: [sec1.p4.s5] None of this prior work is about individuals.
338: [sec1.p4.s6] Perceptions and evaluations of non-living (i.e., abiotic) things are typically studied at the level of the category (e.g., brands; Aaker, 1997), with less attention to individual exemplars (e.g., a specific product).
339: [sec1.p4.s7] Where interpersonal perception research has applied ratings of abiotic individuals, it has used them to approximate scale-use bias (Rau et al., 2021) but not as a phenomenon in its own right.
340: [sec1.p4.s8] Thus, the psychology of perceptions of abiotic individuals, and of individual perceiver differences therein, is largely unclear.
341: [sec1.p4.s9] Whether a perceiver can differentiate abiotic individuals from another, how much liking of certain abiotic individuals is unique to or shared among perceivers, how aware perceivers are of their preferences for certain abiotic individuals, and how much individual perceivers differ in accuracy and awareness are all open empirical questions.
342: [sec1.p4.s10] In the current research, we explore these questions by transferring the methodology established in interpersonal perception research to perceptions of abiotic individuals.
343: [sec1.p4.s11] In doing so, we focus on perceptions of individual gummy bears (i.e., gummy bears of different flavors).
344: [sec1.p4.s12] Gummy bears are particularly well-suited because (a) individuals are near-identical and reproducible in unlimited numbers, (b) cuteness, texture, size, and shape are held
345: 
346: [sec1.p5.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 5 constant by manufacture, and (c) the color-to-flavor mapping is industrially stable and familiar to experienced gummy bear eaters.
347: [sec1.p5.s2] An individual, in the present case, is a gummy bear of a given flavor, met in many near-identical copies.
348: [sec1.p5.s3] The six flavors are therefore the individuals of this study and not categories above them.
349: [sec1.p5.s4] Psychological research has used gummy bears almost only as instruments, as rewards, reinforcers, and divisible stakes (Melis et al., 2015; Sutter et al., 2015), and only rarely regarding flavor recognition (Miyaoka et al., 2018), without systematic analyses of individual differences in accuracy, unique liking, and liking awareness.
350: [sec1.p5.s5] Regarding accuracy in differentiating gummy bear flavors, it is hard to derive any a priori expectations.
351: [sec1.p5.s6] The existing literature on cued identification suggests rather high levels of accuracy for the identification of defined smells.
352: [sec1.p5.s7] For example, adults identified odorants among six named alternatives (chance level 16.7%) in about 76% of trials (de Wijk & Cain, 1994), and the four-alternative Sniffin' Sticks test (chance level 25%) yields about 85% in healthy adults (Oleszkiewicz et al., 2019).
353: [sec1.p5.s8] Research on the accuracy of personality judgments suggests a substantially lower accuracy, with correlations between individual perceiver judgments and actual target personality scores typically ranging between .10 and .30 (translating to 55%-65% accuracy for dichotomous choices), with large variation depending on the trait being judged and the judgment context (Back & Nestler, 2016).
354: [sec1.p5.s9] Recent research on the discrimination of introverted and extraverted targets based on face photographs found an accuracy of 51.1% in a two-alternative forced choice, that is, at the 50% chance level (Jaeger et al., 2024).
355: [sec1.p5.s10] Similarly low levels of 54%, again against a 50% chance level, have been found for lie-truth discrimination (Bond & DePaulo, 2006).
356: [sec1.p5.s11] Beyond average accuracy, we systematically explore contributions of the perceiver (more or less accurate gummy bear judges), target (more or less easy to identify gummy bear flavors), and perceiver-target
357: 
358: [sec1.p6.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 6 interaction (more or less expertise in judging particular flavors; Funder, 1995; Rogers & Biesanz, 2019).
359: [sec1.p6.s2] Regarding unique liking, we transfer the componential nature of interpersonal perceptions (Kenny & La Voie, 1984; Back & Kenny, 2010) to gummy bear perceptions.
360: [sec1.p6.s3] In the same way liking of other human individuals consists of perceiver components (differences in being a liker), target (differences in popularity), and relationship components (differences in unique liking; Back et al., 2011; Dufner & Krause, 2023; Eastwick & Hunt, 2014), gummy bear perceptions can be separated into a perceiver component (differences in the tendency to like gummy bears in general), a target component (differences in the popularity of gummy bear flavors), and a relationship component (the unique gummy bear liking that is due to the particular perceiver-gummy bear pairing).
361: [sec1.p6.s4] Across relational contexts, relationship variance is the largest component when it comes to interpersonal attraction and liking (see Back et al., 2023, for an overview).
362: [sec1.p6.s5] That is, unique taste for specific other human individuals is particularly prevalent.
363: [sec1.p6.s6] Even for something as widely shared as judgments of facial attractiveness, private taste can be as strong as shared taste (Hönekopp, 2006).
364: [sec1.p6.s7] Whether this also holds for the liking of gummy bears is unclear.
365: [sec1.p6.s8] Regarding awareness of one's own unique liking, interpersonal perception research paints a relatively clear picture: People tend to be bad at it: Stated ideals predict evaluations of hypothetical partners but lose that validity for partners actually encountered (Eastwick et al., 2014), and the fit between a person's stated ideals and their realized evaluations is negligible (Sparks et al., 2020).
366: [sec1.p6.s9] Preliminary evidence suggests that this might also hold for non-living individuals: Most people fail to notice when the jam they chose is replaced by a clearly different one (Hall et al., 2010).
367: [sec1.p6.s10] Attitude research points in the same direction: a dissociation of the degree of explicitly stated prejudice toward a category of individuals and the actually expressed prejudiced behavior toward an individual member of that group (Glasman &
368: 
369: [sec1.p7.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 7 Albarracín, 2006; Kurdi et al., 2019; LaPiere, 1934).
370: [sec1.p7.s2] Contact changes attitudes when members cannot be processed as instances of a category (Brewer & Miller, 1984; Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006).
371: [sec1.p7.s3] Similar principles could apply to the perception of gummy bears.
372: [sec1.p7.s4] A stated preference for a gummy bear flavor is also an attitude toward a label that is primarily driven by color (“the red ones”).
373: [sec1.p7.s5] Color preferences track the average affective value of the objects a person associates with a color rather than any property of the wavelength (Palmer & Schloss, 2010), and they can dominate flavor expectations and override the aroma (Morrot et al., 2001; Spence, 2015).
374: [sec1.p7.s6] A gummy bear drawn color-blind into the gummy bear eater's mouth arrives without its label, and it is an open question how much actual taste preferences during such encounters with individual gummy bears correspond with explicitly stated general preferences for certain gummy bear flavors.
375: [sec1.p7.s7] In this study, we provide a first exploration of individual differences in the perception of abiotic individuals, focusing on gummy bears.
376: [sec1.p7.s8] We ask three questions.
377: [sec1.p7.s9] (1) Can perceivers identify gummy bears of different flavors in their mouths, and do they differ in accuracy?
378: [sec1.p7.s10] (2) Does the variance in how much a bear is liked sit in the gummy bear eater (differences in how much perceivers like gummy bears in general), in the gummy bear (differences in how much certain gummy bear flavors are liked), or in their unique pairing (specific preference of a certain gummy bear eater for certain gummy bear flavors)?
379: [sec1.p7.s11] (3) Do gummy bear eaters know their own unique preferences, and do they differ in this knowledge?
380: [sec1.p7.s12] We also explore the possibility of systematic age differences, since adults showed stronger smell identification accuracy (Doty et al., 1984; Oleszkiewicz et al., 2019) and children weighted color, the cue we removed, more heavily than flavor (Oram et al., 1995).
381: [sec1.p7.s13] Open Practices Statement This study is exploratory and was not preregistered.
382: [sec1.p7.s14] Every analysis reported here was specified after the data had been collected and inspected, and all results are labeled
383: 
384: [sec1.p8.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 8 accordingly.
385: [sec1.p8.s2] We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in the study.
386: [sec1.p8.s3] There were no exclusions and no manipulations: all 100 trials from all four participants were included in the analyses.
387: [sec1.p8.s4] Inference relies on effect sizes, exact intervals, and permutation tests rather than on asymptotic approximations.
388: [sec1.p8.s5] The raw data, the analysis-ready data files, the codebook, the analysis code, and the figuregeneration code are openly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22163083 (Förster et al., 2026).
389: [sec1.p8.s6] All analyses are reproduced from one script with a fixed seed, and all figures and supplementary tables are regenerated from the locked data files with one command.
390: [sec1.p8.s7] Materials were commercially available Haribo Goldbears (Haribo Goldbären), all of which were eaten in the course of the study.
391: [sec1.p8.s8] Method Participants Four members of one household took part: two children, aged 8 and 13, and two adults, aged 42 and 47 at the time of data collection in August 2024.
392: [sec1.p8.s9] Three participants were female, and one was male.
393: [sec1.p8.s10] All four are native speakers of German, all four are authors of this report, and all four had eaten Haribo Goldbears before, in quantities none of them recorded.
394: [sec1.p8.s11] We conducted no power analysis before data collection.
395: [sec1.p8.s12] Sample size was determined by the number of people in the household.
396: [sec1.p8.s13] We selected the sample on co-residence and on being on holiday together, which are the only two selection criteria we can state precisely.
397: [sec1.p8.s14] The four perceivers are not independent observations: they share a household, a diet, a shopping pattern, and a history of joint gummy bear consumption, and two of them are the children of the other two.
398: [sec1.p8.s15] Age is fully confounded with person, because exactly one participant occupies each age, and with everything else that distinguishes an 8-year-old from a 47-year-old.
399: [sec1.p8.s16] Two
400: 
401: [sec1.p9.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 9 of the four designed the study and conducted the analyses.
402: [sec1.p9.s2] Every estimate reported below describes these four people.
403: [sec1.p9.s3] We sought no ethics approval.
404: [sec1.p9.s4] The study began as a holiday activity and was written up afterwards.
405: [sec1.p9.s5] The two adults consented to participation and to publication.
406: [sec1.p9.s6] The two minors gave assent, with parental consent from the two adults, and both later read and approved the manuscript.
407: [sec1.p9.s7] The gummy bears did not consent.
408: [sec1.p9.s8] Materials Stimuli were Haribo Goldbears from two 175 g packages, both bought in Italy in August 2024.
409: [sec1.p9.s9] Both packages held the standard German Goldbears product as distributed in the Italian market.
410: [sec1.p9.s10] The product contains six flavors, printed on the package: strawberry, orange, apple, raspberry, lemon, and pineapple.
411: [sec1.p9.s11] Each flavor corresponds to one color, although the strawberry and raspberry shades are less visually distinct than the others.
412: [sec1.p9.s12] Color was not perceivable to the test person at any point during a trial (see Procedure), so the color-to-flavor mapping was a property of the stimulus material and not an available cue.
413: [sec1.p9.s13] The manufacturer does not declare the flavor composition of a package, and we did not count the packages before use.
414: [sec1.p9.s14] Bears were drawn without replacement and eaten, so the realized flavor frequencies reflect package composition and sampling jointly: apple was administered on 23 trials, orange, raspberry, and lemon on 17 each, pineapple on 15, and strawberry on 11.
415: [sec1.p9.s15] A goodness-of-fit test against equal frequencies did not reject uniformity, χ²(5) = 4.52, p = .477.
416: [sec1.p9.s16] We kept both packages in the refrigerator throughout (outdoor temperature at the Italian location averaged approximately 30 °C) and took them out approximately 10 minutes before each session, so bear temperature rose across the five rounds of a session by an unmeasured amount; we measured neither refrigerator temperature nor bear temperature at administration.
417: 
418: [sec1.p10.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 10 Package 1 supplied trials 1 to 72, package 2 trials 73 to 100, with the changeover falling between rounds 3 and 4 of session 4.
419: [sec1.p10.s2] Procedure We ran five sessions on five days: 5, 6, 8, and 9 August 2024 at a holiday location in Italy, and 18 August 2024 at home in Germany.
420: [sec1.p10.s3] Each session consisted of five rounds in a single sitting, and each round consisted of one trial for each of the four participants in the fixed order Ada, Ella, Natalie, Mitja.
421: [sec1.p10.s4] This gives 25 trials per person and 100 trials in total, with no missing data.
422: [sec1.p10.s5] The number of trials per participant was determined pragmatically by the number of days available and the amount of gummy bear consumption deemed acceptable by the parents.
423: [sec1.p10.s6] Time of day was not recorded.
424: [sec1.p10.s7] Session, package, and country breakdowns are given in Table S5.
425: [sec1.p10.s8] Seating was fixed across all five sessions, so each test person received every bear from the same neighbor.
426: [sec1.p10.s9] The administering person is thus confounded with the test person and cannot be separated as a factor.
427: [sec1.p10.s10] A trial ran as follows.
428: [sec1.p10.s11] The test person closed their eyes.
429: [sec1.p10.s12] The person seated to their right reached into the package without looking, drew one bear, and placed it directly into the test person's mouth.
430: [sec1.p10.s13] The test person thus never saw or handled the bear and had no opportunity to smell it before ingestion.
431: [sec1.p10.s14] Retronasal olfaction during chewing was not blocked with a nose clip.
432: [sec1.p10.s15] Because the administering person drew without looking, selection could not be guided by color.
433: [sec1.p10.s16] That person did see the bear once it was out of the package and therefore knew the correct answer while the test person judged.
434: [sec1.p10.s17] We used no procedure to prevent unintended cueing.
435: [sec1.p10.s18] The test person then gave three judgments aloud, in German, in a fixed order: flavor, then certainty, then liking.
436: [sec1.p10.s19] One of the two adults entered each judgment on a laptop as it was given.
437: [sec1.p10.s20] Response time was unlimited.
438: [sec1.p10.s21] Immediately after the liking judgment, and before the next person's turn, the correct flavor was announced to everyone present.
439: [sec1.p10.s22] All four participants
440: 
441: [sec1.p11.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 11 therefore received corrective feedback on their own 25 trials as the test person.
442: [sec1.p11.s2] Water was freely available between trials, but we prescribed no rinsing protocol.
443: [sec1.p11.s3] Measures Measures collected before tasting.
444: [sec1.p11.s4] These were collected on one occasion before the first tasting session.
445: [sec1.p11.s5] They were stated aloud in the group and entered on a laptop by one of the two adults as they were given, so each participant heard the ratings that preceded their own, and the ratings are not independent.
446: [sec1.p11.s6] Predicted accuracy.
447: [sec1.p11.s7] For each of the six flavors, each participant predicted the percentage of trials on which they would identify that flavor correctly, from 0 (no judgments correct) to 100 (all judgments correct).
448: [sec1.p11.s8] The average of these six values is each participant's overall predicted accuracy: 60.0 (age 8), 62.8 (13), 31.3 (42), and 31.3 (47).
449: [sec1.p11.s9] Stated liking.
450: [sec1.p11.s10] Each participant rated how much they like each of the six flavors, from 1 (gar nicht, not at all) to 6 (super gerne, like it very much).
451: [sec1.p11.s11] This rating, given with the flavor name available and before any blind tasting, is the study's measure of stated preference.
452: [sec1.p11.s12] Additional measures collected and not analyzed.
453: [sec1.p11.s13] On the same occasion, each participant also estimated the overall accuracy across flavors of each of the four participants, including themselves, on the 0 to 100 scale, and rated their liking of gummy bears in general on the 1 to 6 scale.
454: [sec1.p11.s14] Both items ask at the general level what the per-flavor items ask more precisely, so the analyses use the per-flavor measures throughout and average across the six flavors wherever an overall value from before the tasting is needed.
455: [sec1.p11.s15] The general liking item has no variance: all four participants gave 3.
456: [sec1.p11.s16] Both measures are included in the openly archived data.
457: [sec1.p11.s17] Per-trial measures.
458: [sec1.p11.s18] Flavor judgment.
459: [sec1.p11.s19] Six-alternative forced choice among the six flavors named above.
460: [sec1.p11.s20] The flavor set was known to all four participants before the first trial and was printed on the package, so chance accuracy is 1/6 = 16.7%.
461: [sec1.p11.s21] Guessing was permitted, and no response could be withheld.
462: 
463: [sec1.p12.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 12 Certainty.
464: [sec1.p12.s2] The rating of how certain the test person was about the flavor judgment was given on a scale from 1 (sehr unsicher, very uncertain) to 6 (sehr sicher, very certain).
465: [sec1.p12.s3] Tasted liking.
466: [sec1.p12.s4] How much the test person liked the gummy bear just tasted was also rated from 1 (gar nicht lecker, not tasty at all) to 6 (super lecker, very tasty).
467: [sec1.p12.s5] This blind, per-trial rating is the study's measure of experienced preference.
468: [sec1.p12.s6] Identification accuracy.
469: [sec1.p12.s7] A trial was scored 1 when the flavor named matched the flavor administered and 0 otherwise.
470: [sec1.p12.s8] The administering person scored each trial at the moment of feedback, and the data were entered into the laptop right away.
471: [sec1.p12.s9] The scoring requires no coder judgment, and we verified that the recorded accuracy variable reproduces the comparison of named and administered flavor on all 100 trials.
472: [sec1.p12.s10] Design and Analysis Each perceiver judged bears of every flavor but the bears judged nothing, so the design is fully crossed in one direction only (a half-block design; Biesanz, 2010; Kenny et al., 2006; see also Stecker et al., 2021).
473: [sec1.p12.s11] Because each perceiver tasted each flavor between one and eight times, the perceiver x flavor component of the per-trial judgments is separable from trial-level error, which requires repeated ratings per cell (Xie et al., 2019); with one rating per perceiver-target pair, that component stays inside the residual.
474: [sec1.p12.s12] The variance decompositions follow the logic of the social relations model but are estimated as a plain two-way decomposition of the 4 x 6 matrix of cell means.
475: [sec1.p12.s13] Round-robin estimating equations subtract the expected sampling-noise contribution from each variance component analytically; our design does not meet their assumptions, with two modes, cell sizes of 1 to 8, and a binary accuracy outcome, so we subtract noise floors simulated under the observed design instead.
476: [sec1.p12.s14] Raw, floor, and corrected values for every component are reported in Table S10.
477: [sec1.p12.s15] We rely on permutation and exact tests throughout.
478: [sec1.p12.s16] We report the variance decompositions descriptively and interpret only the ordering of the components, because random-effect
479: 
480: [sec1.p13.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 13 variances estimated from four perceivers and six flavors are unstable by construction (McNeish & Stapleton, 2016).
481: [sec1.p13.s2] Crossed random-effects models with random intercepts for perceiver, flavor, and their interaction (Judd et al., 2012) accompany every decomposition as control variables.
482: [sec1.p13.s3] All of them reach singular fits, which is expected at these cluster counts and does not indicate that a variance is zero (Matuschek et al., 2017; Table S13).
483: [sec1.p13.s4] Primary analyses were run in Python 3.10.12 (pandas 2.3.3, numpy 2.2.6, scipy 1.15.3); control analyses were run in R 4.5.3 (lme4 2.0-6, pROC 1.19.0.1), with the agreement between the two pipelines documented in Table S13.
484: [sec1.p13.s5] Results Preliminary Analyses Unless noted otherwise, intervals are Clopper-Pearson exact 95% intervals, binomial tests are exact and two-sided against 1/6, and permutation tests use 10,000 draws, with p computed as (1 + the number of draws at least as extreme as the observed value) / 10,001, so the smallest attainable value is 1/10001 and is reported as p < .001.
485: [sec1.p13.s6] Tables 1 and 2 report descriptives at every level the design affords; session, package, and country breakdowns are in Table S5.
486: [sec1.p13.s7] Accuracy did not improve across trials.
487: [sec1.p13.s8] The association between outcome and the number of prior feedback occasions on the same flavor, stratified by perceiver x flavor cell, was flat (r_strat = .04, p = .83), as were the global-time variant (r_strat = .03, p = .81) and every perperceiver test (Table S6, Figure S2).
488: [sec1.p13.s9] Thus, no analysis reported below carries a trial-order covariate.
489: [sec1.p13.s10] The two perceivers who ended accurately were accurate from the start, with 9 of 12 and 8 of 12 correct in their first halves (Figure S2B; pooled halves 22/48 against 20/52, Table S6).

513: [sec1.p16.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 16 Accurate Differentiation Pooled accuracy, the proportion of trials correctly identified, was 42 of 100, .42 [.32, .52]; that interval treats the 100 trials as independent, which they are not, since they come from four perceivers.
514: [sec1.p16.s2] Perceivers differed strongly: two of the four identified flavors far above chance and two did not (Figure 1A), χ²(3) = 21.51, exact conditional p < .001 (Table S1).
515: [sec1.p16.s3] Ella named 17 of 25 correctly, .68 [.46, .85], p < .001, and Mitja 15 of 25, .60 [.39, .79], p < .001, against Natalie's 7 of 25, .28 [.12, .49], p = .17, and Ada's 3 of 25, .12 [.03, .31], p = .79.
516: [sec1.p16.s4] Ada's .12 lies below the chance line descriptively, but we read her performance as guessing.
517: [sec1.p16.s5] Only zero hits in 25 trials would reject downward (one-sided p = .010).
518: [sec1.p16.s6] Detecting a true accuracy of .05 or .10 against the 1/6 chance level with 80% power would take about 45 or 163 trials per perceiver, respectively.
519: [sec1.p16.s7] At this point, parental concerns about Ada's health outweighed concerns about statistical power.
520: [sec1.p16.s8] Mapped onto age, accuracy was .12 at age 8, .68 at 13, .28 at 42, and .60 at 47.
521: [sec1.p16.s9] The pattern is non-monotonic.
522: [sec1.p16.s10] Its within-generation spread exceeds its between-generation differences, and it does not support a systematic age effect.

534: [sec1.p18.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 18 The most frequent confusions (see Figure 1B) were lemon named orange (6 trials), apple named raspberry (6), orange named lemon (5), and pineapple named lemon (4).
535: [sec1.p18.s2] Per-flavor accuracy pooled over perceivers ran from .33 for pineapple to .53 for orange and raspberry (Tables S1, S2).
536: [sec1.p18.s3] Some of these pooled confusions resemble within-fruit confusions reported in cued identification research (Brandão et al., 2025).
537: [sec1.p18.s4] However, most errors in the pooled matrix came from the two less accurate gummy bear judges, so this pattern cannot establish sensory confusability.
538: [sec1.p18.s5] Figure 1C gives one-versus-rest discrimination for all 24 perceiver x flavor cells, as rankbased areas under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC) of a certaintygraded score that considers both sensitivity (the ability of a perceiver to detect a gummy bear flavor when eating one) and specificity (the ability of a perceiver to not name a gummy bear flavor when not eating one).
539: [sec1.p18.s6] The certainty-graded models were warranted given that certainty carried relevant signal, at least for some of the perceivers: Certainty discriminated correct from incorrect trials for Ella (AUC = .95, p < .001) and Mitja (.79, p = .005) but not for Natalie (.56, p = .37) or Ada (.38 on three correct trials, p = .81; Table S7).
540: [sec1.p18.s7] Cells rest on 1 to 8 positive trials, which is why the figure prints each cell's n.
541: [sec1.p18.s8] Macro-averaged within perceiver, Ella reached .95 in identification and Mitja .85, both at one-sided permutation p < .001, against .50 for Natalie (p = .46) and .40 for Ada (p = .94).
542: [sec1.p18.s9] The grand macro-AUC was .68 (p < .001), and per-flavor macro-AUCs ran from .56 for lemon (p = .27) to .83 for raspberry (p < .001; see Table S8, Figure S3).
543: [sec1.p18.s10] To compare the found identification values with those in the literature, we rescaled the hit rate at k alternatives onto an index whose null value is .50 regardless of k (Rosenthal & Rubin, 1989; Tskhay & Rule, 2013).
544: [sec1.p18.s11] Our pooled .42 at six alternatives becomes π = .78, against .51 for picking the more extraverted of two faces (Jaeger et al., 2024), .54 for detecting deception (Bond & DePaulo, 2006), and .88 or higher for cued flavor and odor
545: 
546: [sec1.p19.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 19 identification; the index equalizes the number of alternatives and not the difficulty of the task, and the anosmia cut-off of the Candy Smell Test, a four-alternative retronasal test (Renner et al., 2009), rescales to π = .80, just above our own value (Table S14).
547: [sec1.p19.s2] On the discrimination metric, the grand macro-AUC of .68 corresponds under an equal-variance binormal model to d = 0.66 and an effect-size-equivalent r = .31 (Rice & Harris, 2005).
548: [sec1.p19.s3] Reported mean singlejudge first-impression accuracy is r = .25 (Carney et al., 2007), and self-stranger agreement runs from .08 to .28 (Connelly & Ones, 2010, Table 5 and Table 9).
549: [sec1.p19.s4] Table S14 sets out the forced-choice benchmarks with their raw values, numbers of alternatives, and chance levels, and its note gives the conversion behind the discrimination-metric values.

[sec1.p1.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 1 Individual differences in the perception of abiotic individuals: The case of gummy bears Natalie Förster1, Ella Back2, Ada M. Förster2, and Mitja D. Back3 1University of Wuppertal, Institute for Educational Research, Germany 2 independent researcher 3University of Münster, Department of Psychology, Germany Preprint, 29 August 2026.
[sec1.p1.s2] Not peer reviewed.
[sec1.p1.s3] Please cite as Förster, N., Back, E., Förster, A. M., & Back, M. D. (2026).
[sec1.p1.s4] Individual differences in the perception of abiotic individuals: The case of gummy bears.
[sec1.p1.s5] Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22163292

[sec1.p2.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 2 Abstract People routinely perceive and evaluate things that are not alive, yet research on those perceptions and evaluations has focused on the level of the category (e.g., perceiving flowers, wine, food, artwork).
[sec1.p2.s2] Here we translate research on interpersonal perception to abiotic individuals and investigate individual differences between human perceivers in the accurate perception of and their unique preferences for gummy bear individuals of different flavors.
[sec1.p2.s3] Four members of one family, aged 8 to 47, each tasted 25 gummy bears drawn blind (100 trials in total).
[sec1.p2.s4] On each trial, the participant named the flavor among six known alternatives (strawberry, orange, apple, raspberry, lemon, pineapple), rated their certainty, and indicated their liking for the gummy bear.
[sec1.p2.s5] Liking for each flavor had also been stated before the tasting trials.
[sec1.p2.s6] Average accuracy in gummy bear identification (42%) was well above chance level (16.7%), with large interindividual variability (individual accuracies ranged from 12% to 68%).
[sec1.p2.s7] While stated liking was largely consensual between the family members, tasted liking was driven by the unique perceiver x flavor pairing.
[sec1.p2.s8] Also, stated preferences did not track tasted ones on average, and the correspondence varied widely across the four perceivers.
[sec1.p2.s9] Results underline the existence of individual differences in accurate perceptions of and unique preferences for gummy bears and point to fruitful avenues for future research on the perception of abiotic individuals in general.
[sec1.p2.s10] Keywords: interpersonal perception, individual differences, flavor identification, accuracy, uniqueness, gummy bears

[sec1.p3.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 3 Statement of Relevance People spend a great deal of their lives evaluating things that are not people: foods, products, objects, media.
[sec1.p3.s2] Psychology usually measures these evaluations at the level of the category, by asking which flavors, brands, or designs a person prefers.
[sec1.p3.s3] We measured what happens one level down, when a person meets a single member of a category without knowing which category it belongs to, in this case a gummy bear of unknown flavor placed directly in the mouth.
[sec1.p3.s4] What our participants said about the flavors in advance agreed well across family members, but the two flavors they named as best beforehand were not the two they liked best in the mouth.
[sec1.p3.s5] How well they could identify what they were eating also differed sharply from person to person.
[sec1.p3.s6] Two of the four could name the gummy bear flavor in their mouth far more often than guessing would allow, and two were found to be bad gummy bear judges.
[sec1.p3.s7] Surveys, menus, gift choices, and reward schemes for children all assume that a stated preference for a category describes the experience of its members.
[sec1.p3.s8] Measuring that experience directly is feasible, and it gives a different answer.

[sec1.p4.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 4 Introduction "I only like the red ones!
[sec1.p4.s2] (Anonymous, 8 years) People form perceptions of things that are not alive as readily as they form perceptions of one another.
[sec1.p4.s3] Processes similar to those that characterize perceptions between humans can not only be found for human perceptions of animals (Gosling et al., 2003), but they also run across perceptions of machines and other objects, stopping at no clear boundary (Epley et al., 2007; Gray et al., 2007).
[sec1.p4.s4] The degree to which human-like perceptions are applied to objects varies across human perceivers (Waytz et al., 2010) with consequences for how much individuals are attached to these objects (Chandler & Schwarz, 2010).
[sec1.p4.s5] None of this prior work is about individuals.
[sec1.p4.s6] Perceptions and evaluations of non-living (i.e., abiotic) things are typically studied at the level of the category (e.g., brands; Aaker, 1997), with less attention to individual exemplars (e.g., a specific product).
[sec1.p4.s7] Where interpersonal perception research has applied ratings of abiotic individuals, it has used them to approximate scale-use bias (Rau et al., 2021) but not as a phenomenon in its own right.
[sec1.p4.s8] Thus, the psychology of perceptions of abiotic individuals, and of individual perceiver differences therein, is largely unclear.
[sec1.p4.s9] Whether a perceiver can differentiate abiotic individuals from another, how much liking of certain abiotic individuals is unique to or shared among perceivers, how aware perceivers are of their preferences for certain abiotic individuals, and how much individual perceivers differ in accuracy and awareness are all open empirical questions.
[sec1.p4.s10] In the current research, we explore these questions by transferring the methodology established in interpersonal perception research to perceptions of abiotic individuals.
[sec1.p4.s11] In doing so, we focus on perceptions of individual gummy bears (i.e., gummy bears of different flavors).
[sec1.p4.s12] Gummy bears are particularly well-suited because (a) individuals are near-identical and reproducible in unlimited numbers, (b) cuteness, texture, size, and shape are held

[sec1.p5.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 5 constant by manufacture, and (c) the color-to-flavor mapping is industrially stable and familiar to experienced gummy bear eaters.
[sec1.p5.s2] An individual, in the present case, is a gummy bear of a given flavor, met in many near-identical copies.
[sec1.p5.s3] The six flavors are therefore the individuals of this study and not categories above them.
[sec1.p5.s4] Psychological research has used gummy bears almost only as instruments, as rewards, reinforcers, and divisible stakes (Melis et al., 2015; Sutter et al., 2015), and only rarely regarding flavor recognition (Miyaoka et al., 2018), without systematic analyses of individual differences in accuracy, unique liking, and liking awareness.
[sec1.p5.s5] Regarding accuracy in differentiating gummy bear flavors, it is hard to derive any a priori expectations.
[sec1.p5.s6] The existing literature on cued identification suggests rather high levels of accuracy for the identification of defined smells.
[sec1.p5.s7] For example, adults identified odorants among six named alternatives (chance level 16.7%) in about 76% of trials (de Wijk & Cain, 1994), and the four-alternative Sniffin' Sticks test (chance level 25%) yields about 85% in healthy adults (Oleszkiewicz et al., 2019).
[sec1.p5.s8] Research on the accuracy of personality judgments suggests a substantially lower accuracy, with correlations between individual perceiver judgments and actual target personality scores typically ranging between .10 and .30 (translating to 55%-65% accuracy for dichotomous choices), with large variation depending on the trait being judged and the judgment context (Back & Nestler, 2016).
[sec1.p5.s9] Recent research on the discrimination of introverted and extraverted targets based on face photographs found an accuracy of 51.1% in a two-alternative forced choice, that is, at the 50% chance level (Jaeger et al., 2024).
[sec1.p5.s10] Similarly low levels of 54%, again against a 50% chance level, have been found for lie-truth discrimination (Bond & DePaulo, 2006).
[sec1.p5.s11] Beyond average accuracy, we systematically explore contributions of the perceiver (more or less accurate gummy bear judges), target (more or less easy to identify gummy bear flavors), and perceiver-target

[sec1.p6.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 6 interaction (more or less expertise in judging particular flavors; Funder, 1995; Rogers & Biesanz, 2019).
[sec1.p6.s2] Regarding unique liking, we transfer the componential nature of interpersonal perceptions (Kenny & La Voie, 1984; Back & Kenny, 2010) to gummy bear perceptions.
[sec1.p6.s3] In the same way liking of other human individuals consists of perceiver components (differences in being a liker), target (differences in popularity), and relationship components (differences in unique liking; Back et al., 2011; Dufner & Krause, 2023; Eastwick & Hunt, 2014), gummy bear perceptions can be separated into a perceiver component (differences in the tendency to like gummy bears in general), a target component (differences in the popularity of gummy bear flavors), and a relationship component (the unique gummy bear liking that is due to the particular perceiver-gummy bear pairing).
[sec1.p6.s4] Across relational contexts, relationship variance is the largest component when it comes to interpersonal attraction and liking (see Back et al., 2023, for an overview).
[sec1.p6.s5] That is, unique taste for specific other human individuals is particularly prevalent.
[sec1.p6.s6] Even for something as widely shared as judgments of facial attractiveness, private taste can be as strong as shared taste (Hönekopp, 2006).
[sec1.p6.s7] Whether this also holds for the liking of gummy bears is unclear.
[sec1.p6.s8] Regarding awareness of one's own unique liking, interpersonal perception research paints a relatively clear picture: People tend to be bad at it: Stated ideals predict evaluations of hypothetical partners but lose that validity for partners actually encountered (Eastwick et al., 2014), and the fit between a person's stated ideals and their realized evaluations is negligible (Sparks et al., 2020).
[sec1.p6.s9] Preliminary evidence suggests that this might also hold for non-living individuals: Most people fail to notice when the jam they chose is replaced by a clearly different one (Hall et al., 2010).
[sec1.p6.s10] Attitude research points in the same direction: a dissociation of the degree of explicitly stated prejudice toward a category of individuals and the actually expressed prejudiced behavior toward an individual member of that group (Glasman &

[sec1.p7.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 7 Albarracín, 2006; Kurdi et al., 2019; LaPiere, 1934).
[sec1.p7.s2] Contact changes attitudes when members cannot be processed as instances of a category (Brewer & Miller, 1984; Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006).
[sec1.p7.s3] Similar principles could apply to the perception of gummy bears.
[sec1.p7.s4] A stated preference for a gummy bear flavor is also an attitude toward a label that is primarily driven by color (“the red ones”).
[sec1.p7.s5] Color preferences track the average affective value of the objects a person associates with a color rather than any property of the wavelength (Palmer & Schloss, 2010), and they can dominate flavor expectations and override the aroma (Morrot et al., 2001; Spence, 2015).
[sec1.p7.s6] A gummy bear drawn color-blind into the gummy bear eater's mouth arrives without its label, and it is an open question how much actual taste preferences during such encounters with individual gummy bears correspond with explicitly stated general preferences for certain gummy bear flavors.
[sec1.p7.s7] In this study, we provide a first exploration of individual differences in the perception of abiotic individuals, focusing on gummy bears.
[sec1.p7.s8] We ask three questions.
[sec1.p7.s9] (1) Can perceivers identify gummy bears of different flavors in their mouths, and do they differ in accuracy?
[sec1.p7.s10] (2) Does the variance in how much a bear is liked sit in the gummy bear eater (differences in how much perceivers like gummy bears in general), in the gummy bear (differences in how much certain gummy bear flavors are liked), or in their unique pairing (specific preference of a certain gummy bear eater for certain gummy bear flavors)?
[sec1.p7.s11] (3) Do gummy bear eaters know their own unique preferences, and do they differ in this knowledge?
[sec1.p7.s12] We also explore the possibility of systematic age differences, since adults showed stronger smell identification accuracy (Doty et al., 1984; Oleszkiewicz et al., 2019) and children weighted color, the cue we removed, more heavily than flavor (Oram et al., 1995).
[sec1.p7.s13] Open Practices Statement This study is exploratory and was not preregistered.
[sec1.p7.s14] Every analysis reported here was specified after the data had been collected and inspected, and all results are labeled

[sec1.p8.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 8 accordingly.
[sec1.p8.s2] We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in the study.
[sec1.p8.s3] There were no exclusions and no manipulations: all 100 trials from all four participants were included in the analyses.
[sec1.p8.s4] Inference relies on effect sizes, exact intervals, and permutation tests rather than on asymptotic approximations.
[sec1.p8.s5] The raw data, the analysis-ready data files, the codebook, the analysis code, and the figuregeneration code are openly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22163083 (Förster et al., 2026).
[sec1.p8.s6] All analyses are reproduced from one script with a fixed seed, and all figures and supplementary tables are regenerated from the locked data files with one command.
[sec1.p8.s7] Materials were commercially available Haribo Goldbears (Haribo Goldbären), all of which were eaten in the course of the study.
[sec1.p8.s8] Method Participants Four members of one household took part: two children, aged 8 and 13, and two adults, aged 42 and 47 at the time of data collection in August 2024.
[sec1.p8.s9] Three participants were female, and one was male.
[sec1.p8.s10] All four are native speakers of German, all four are authors of this report, and all four had eaten Haribo Goldbears before, in quantities none of them recorded.
[sec1.p8.s11] We conducted no power analysis before data collection.
[sec1.p8.s12] Sample size was determined by the number of people in the household.
[sec1.p8.s13] We selected the sample on co-residence and on being on holiday together, which are the only two selection criteria we can state precisely.
[sec1.p8.s14] The four perceivers are not independent observations: they share a household, a diet, a shopping pattern, and a history of joint gummy bear consumption, and two of them are the children of the other two.
[sec1.p8.s15] Age is fully confounded with person, because exactly one participant occupies each age, and with everything else that distinguishes an 8-year-old from a 47-year-old.
[sec1.p8.s16] Two

[sec1.p9.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 9 of the four designed the study and conducted the analyses.
[sec1.p9.s2] Every estimate reported below describes these four people.
[sec1.p9.s3] We sought no ethics approval.
[sec1.p9.s4] The study began as a holiday activity and was written up afterwards.
[sec1.p9.s5] The two adults consented to participation and to publication.
[sec1.p9.s6] The two minors gave assent, with parental consent from the two adults, and both later read and approved the manuscript.
[sec1.p9.s7] The gummy bears did not consent.
[sec1.p9.s8] Materials Stimuli were Haribo Goldbears from two 175 g packages, both bought in Italy in August 2024.
[sec1.p9.s9] Both packages held the standard German Goldbears product as distributed in the Italian market.
[sec1.p9.s10] The product contains six flavors, printed on the package: strawberry, orange, apple, raspberry, lemon, and pineapple.
[sec1.p9.s11] Each flavor corresponds to one color, although the strawberry and raspberry shades are less visually distinct than the others.
[sec1.p9.s12] Color was not perceivable to the test person at any point during a trial (see Procedure), so the color-to-flavor mapping was a property of the stimulus material and not an available cue.
[sec1.p9.s13] The manufacturer does not declare the flavor composition of a package, and we did not count the packages before use.
[sec1.p9.s14] Bears were drawn without replacement and eaten, so the realized flavor frequencies reflect package composition and sampling jointly: apple was administered on 23 trials, orange, raspberry, and lemon on 17 each, pineapple on 15, and strawberry on 11.
[sec1.p9.s15] A goodness-of-fit test against equal frequencies did not reject uniformity, χ²(5) = 4.52, p = .477.
[sec1.p9.s16] We kept both packages in the refrigerator throughout (outdoor temperature at the Italian location averaged approximately 30 °C) and took them out approximately 10 minutes before each session, so bear temperature rose across the five rounds of a session by an unmeasured amount; we measured neither refrigerator temperature nor bear temperature at administration.

[sec1.p10.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 10 Package 1 supplied trials 1 to 72, package 2 trials 73 to 100, with the changeover falling between rounds 3 and 4 of session 4.
[sec1.p10.s2] Procedure We ran five sessions on five days: 5, 6, 8, and 9 August 2024 at a holiday location in Italy, and 18 August 2024 at home in Germany.
[sec1.p10.s3] Each session consisted of five rounds in a single sitting, and each round consisted of one trial for each of the four participants in the fixed order Ada, Ella, Natalie, Mitja.
[sec1.p10.s4] This gives 25 trials per person and 100 trials in total, with no missing data.
[sec1.p10.s5] The number of trials per participant was determined pragmatically by the number of days available and the amount of gummy bear consumption deemed acceptable by the parents.
[sec1.p10.s6] Time of day was not recorded.
[sec1.p10.s7] Session, package, and country breakdowns are given in Table S5.
[sec1.p10.s8] Seating was fixed across all five sessions, so each test person received every bear from the same neighbor.
[sec1.p10.s9] The administering person is thus confounded with the test person and cannot be separated as a factor.
[sec1.p10.s10] A trial ran as follows.
[sec1.p10.s11] The test person closed their eyes.
[sec1.p10.s12] The person seated to their right reached into the package without looking, drew one bear, and placed it directly into the test person's mouth.
[sec1.p10.s13] The test person thus never saw or handled the bear and had no opportunity to smell it before ingestion.
[sec1.p10.s14] Retronasal olfaction during chewing was not blocked with a nose clip.
[sec1.p10.s15] Because the administering person drew without looking, selection could not be guided by color.
[sec1.p10.s16] That person did see the bear once it was out of the package and therefore knew the correct answer while the test person judged.
[sec1.p10.s17] We used no procedure to prevent unintended cueing.
[sec1.p10.s18] The test person then gave three judgments aloud, in German, in a fixed order: flavor, then certainty, then liking.
[sec1.p10.s19] One of the two adults entered each judgment on a laptop as it was given.
[sec1.p10.s20] Response time was unlimited.
[sec1.p10.s21] Immediately after the liking judgment, and before the next person's turn, the correct flavor was announced to everyone present.
[sec1.p10.s22] All four participants

[sec1.p11.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 11 therefore received corrective feedback on their own 25 trials as the test person.
[sec1.p11.s2] Water was freely available between trials, but we prescribed no rinsing protocol.
[sec1.p11.s3] Measures Measures collected before tasting.
[sec1.p11.s4] These were collected on one occasion before the first tasting session.
[sec1.p11.s5] They were stated aloud in the group and entered on a laptop by one of the two adults as they were given, so each participant heard the ratings that preceded their own, and the ratings are not independent.
[sec1.p11.s6] Predicted accuracy.
[sec1.p11.s7] For each of the six flavors, each participant predicted the percentage of trials on which they would identify that flavor correctly, from 0 (no judgments correct) to 100 (all judgments correct).
[sec1.p11.s8] The average of these six values is each participant's overall predicted accuracy: 60.0 (age 8), 62.8 (13), 31.3 (42), and 31.3 (47).
[sec1.p11.s9] Stated liking.
[sec1.p11.s10] Each participant rated how much they like each of the six flavors, from 1 (gar nicht, not at all) to 6 (super gerne, like it very much).
[sec1.p11.s11] This rating, given with the flavor name available and before any blind tasting, is the study's measure of stated preference.
[sec1.p11.s12] Additional measures collected and not analyzed.
[sec1.p11.s13] On the same occasion, each participant also estimated the overall accuracy across flavors of each of the four participants, including themselves, on the 0 to 100 scale, and rated their liking of gummy bears in general on the 1 to 6 scale.
[sec1.p11.s14] Both items ask at the general level what the per-flavor items ask more precisely, so the analyses use the per-flavor measures throughout and average across the six flavors wherever an overall value from before the tasting is needed.
[sec1.p11.s15] The general liking item has no variance: all four participants gave 3.
[sec1.p11.s16] Both measures are included in the openly archived data.
[sec1.p11.s17] Per-trial measures.
[sec1.p11.s18] Flavor judgment.
[sec1.p11.s19] Six-alternative forced choice among the six flavors named above.
[sec1.p11.s20] The flavor set was known to all four participants before the first trial and was printed on the package, so chance accuracy is 1/6 = 16.7%.
[sec1.p11.s21] Guessing was permitted, and no response could be withheld.

[sec1.p12.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 12 Certainty.
[sec1.p12.s2] The rating of how certain the test person was about the flavor judgment was given on a scale from 1 (sehr unsicher, very uncertain) to 6 (sehr sicher, very certain).
[sec1.p12.s3] Tasted liking.
[sec1.p12.s4] How much the test person liked the gummy bear just tasted was also rated from 1 (gar nicht lecker, not tasty at all) to 6 (super lecker, very tasty).
[sec1.p12.s5] This blind, per-trial rating is the study's measure of experienced preference.
[sec1.p12.s6] Identification accuracy.
[sec1.p12.s7] A trial was scored 1 when the flavor named matched the flavor administered and 0 otherwise.
[sec1.p12.s8] The administering person scored each trial at the moment of feedback, and the data were entered into the laptop right away.
[sec1.p12.s9] The scoring requires no coder judgment, and we verified that the recorded accuracy variable reproduces the comparison of named and administered flavor on all 100 trials.
[sec1.p12.s10] Design and Analysis Each perceiver judged bears of every flavor but the bears judged nothing, so the design is fully crossed in one direction only (a half-block design; Biesanz, 2010; Kenny et al., 2006; see also Stecker et al., 2021).
[sec1.p12.s11] Because each perceiver tasted each flavor between one and eight times, the perceiver x flavor component of the per-trial judgments is separable from trial-level error, which requires repeated ratings per cell (Xie et al., 2019); with one rating per perceiver-target pair, that component stays inside the residual.
[sec1.p12.s12] The variance decompositions follow the logic of the social relations model but are estimated as a plain two-way decomposition of the 4 x 6 matrix of cell means.
[sec1.p12.s13] Round-robin estimating equations subtract the expected sampling-noise contribution from each variance component analytically; our design does not meet their assumptions, with two modes, cell sizes of 1 to 8, and a binary accuracy outcome, so we subtract noise floors simulated under the observed design instead.
[sec1.p12.s14] Raw, floor, and corrected values for every component are reported in Table S10.
[sec1.p12.s15] We rely on permutation and exact tests throughout.
[sec1.p12.s16] We report the variance decompositions descriptively and interpret only the ordering of the components, because random-effect

[sec1.p13.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 13 variances estimated from four perceivers and six flavors are unstable by construction (McNeish & Stapleton, 2016).
[sec1.p13.s2] Crossed random-effects models with random intercepts for perceiver, flavor, and their interaction (Judd et al., 2012) accompany every decomposition as control variables.
[sec1.p13.s3] All of them reach singular fits, which is expected at these cluster counts and does not indicate that a variance is zero (Matuschek et al., 2017; Table S13).
[sec1.p13.s4] Primary analyses were run in Python 3.10.12 (pandas 2.3.3, numpy 2.2.6, scipy 1.15.3); control analyses were run in R 4.5.3 (lme4 2.0-6, pROC 1.19.0.1), with the agreement between the two pipelines documented in Table S13.
[sec1.p13.s5] Results Preliminary Analyses Unless noted otherwise, intervals are Clopper-Pearson exact 95% intervals, binomial tests are exact and two-sided against 1/6, and permutation tests use 10,000 draws, with p computed as (1 + the number of draws at least as extreme as the observed value) / 10,001, so the smallest attainable value is 1/10001 and is reported as p < .001.
[sec1.p13.s6] Tables 1 and 2 report descriptives at every level the design affords; session, package, and country breakdowns are in Table S5.
[sec1.p13.s7] Accuracy did not improve across trials.
[sec1.p13.s8] The association between outcome and the number of prior feedback occasions on the same flavor, stratified by perceiver x flavor cell, was flat (r_strat = .04, p = .83), as were the global-time variant (r_strat = .03, p = .81) and every perperceiver test (Table S6, Figure S2).
[sec1.p13.s9] Thus, no analysis reported below carries a trial-order covariate.
[sec1.p13.s10] The two perceivers who ended accurately were accurate from the start, with 9 of 12 and 8 of 12 correct in their first halves (Figure S2B; pooled halves 22/48 against 20/52, Table S6).
[sec1.p13.s11] The accuracy of a perceiver's trials in one half was closely related to their accuracy in the other half, with a correlation of r = .86 for odd versus even trials and r = .94 for sessions 1 to

[sec1.p14.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 14 3 compared to sessions 4 and 5.
[sec1.p14.s2] These correlations were calculated across the four perceivers (see Table S6).
[sec1.p14.s3] The differences reported next therefore describe stable performance.
[sec1.p14.s4] No perceiver departed from uniform use of the six response options (χ²(5) between 0.68 and 6.44, smallest p = .29), the pooled response distribution was likewise uniform (χ²(5) = 5.00, p = .42), and individual response biases stayed between −.16 and +.16 (Table S3).

[sec1.p16.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 16 Accurate Differentiation Pooled accuracy, the proportion of trials correctly identified, was 42 of 100, .42 [.32, .52]; that interval treats the 100 trials as independent, which they are not, since they come from four perceivers.
[sec1.p16.s2] Perceivers differed strongly: two of the four identified flavors far above chance and two did not (Figure 1A), χ²(3) = 21.51, exact conditional p < .001 (Table S1).
[sec1.p16.s3] Ella named 17 of 25 correctly, .68 [.46, .85], p < .001, and Mitja 15 of 25, .60 [.39, .79], p < .001, against Natalie's 7 of 25, .28 [.12, .49], p = .17, and Ada's 3 of 25, .12 [.03, .31], p = .79.
[sec1.p16.s4] Ada's .12 lies below the chance line descriptively, but we read her performance as guessing.
[sec1.p16.s5] Only zero hits in 25 trials would reject downward (one-sided p = .010).
[sec1.p16.s6] Detecting a true accuracy of .05 or .10 against the 1/6 chance level with 80% power would take about 45 or 163 trials per perceiver, respectively.
[sec1.p16.s7] At this point, parental concerns about Ada's health outweighed concerns about statistical power.
[sec1.p16.s8] Mapped onto age, accuracy was .12 at age 8, .68 at 13, .28 at 42, and .60 at 47.
[sec1.p16.s9] The pattern is non-monotonic.
[sec1.p16.s10] Its within-generation spread exceeds its between-generation differences, and it does not support a systematic age effect.

[sec1.p18.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 18 The most frequent confusions (see Figure 1B) were lemon named orange (6 trials), apple named raspberry (6), orange named lemon (5), and pineapple named lemon (4).
[sec1.p18.s2] Per-flavor accuracy pooled over perceivers ran from .33 for pineapple to .53 for orange and raspberry (Tables S1, S2).
[sec1.p18.s3] Some of these pooled confusions resemble within-fruit confusions reported in cued identification research (Brandão et al., 2025).
[sec1.p18.s4] However, most errors in the pooled matrix came from the two less accurate gummy bear judges, so this pattern cannot establish sensory confusability.
[sec1.p18.s5] Figure 1C gives one-versus-rest discrimination for all 24 perceiver x flavor cells, as rankbased areas under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC) of a certaintygraded score that considers both sensitivity (the ability of a perceiver to detect a gummy bear flavor when eating one) and specificity (the ability of a perceiver to not name a gummy bear flavor when not eating one).
[sec1.p18.s6] The certainty-graded models were warranted given that certainty carried relevant signal, at least for some of the perceivers: Certainty discriminated correct from incorrect trials for Ella (AUC = .95, p < .001) and Mitja (.79, p = .005) but not for Natalie (.56, p = .37) or Ada (.38 on three correct trials, p = .81; Table S7).
[sec1.p18.s7] Cells rest on 1 to 8 positive trials, which is why the figure prints each cell's n.
[sec1.p18.s8] Macro-averaged within perceiver, Ella reached .95 in identification and Mitja .85, both at one-sided permutation p < .001, against .50 for Natalie (p = .46) and .40 for Ada (p = .94).
[sec1.p18.s9] The grand macro-AUC was .68 (p < .001), and per-flavor macro-AUCs ran from .56 for lemon (p = .27) to .83 for raspberry (p < .001; see Table S8, Figure S3).
[sec1.p18.s10] To compare the found identification values with those in the literature, we rescaled the hit rate at k alternatives onto an index whose null value is .50 regardless of k (Rosenthal & Rubin, 1989; Tskhay & Rule, 2013).
[sec1.p18.s11] Our pooled .42 at six alternatives becomes π = .78, against .51 for picking the more extraverted of two faces (Jaeger et al., 2024), .54 for detecting deception (Bond & DePaulo, 2006), and .88 or higher for cued flavor and odor

[sec1.p19.s1] PERCEPTION OF GUMMY BEARS 19 identification; the index equalizes the number of alternatives and not the difficulty of the task, and the anosmia cut-off of the Candy Smell Test, a four-alternative retronasal test (Renner et al., 2009), rescales to π = .80, just above our own value (Table S14).
[sec1.p19.s2] On the discrimination metric, the grand macro-AUC of .68 corresponds under an equal-variance binormal model to d = 0.66 and an effect-size-equivalent r = .31 (Rice & Harris, 2005).
[sec1.p19.s3] Reported mean singlejudge first-impression accuracy is r = .25 (Carney et al., 2007), and self-stranger agreement runs from .08 to .28 (Connelly & Ones, 2010, Table 5 and Table 9).
[sec1.p19.s4] Table S14 sets out the forced-choice benchmarks with their raw values, numbers of alternatives, and chance levels, and its note gives the conversion behind the discrimination-metric values.","lineStart":1,"lineEnd":549,"totalLines":550,"truncated":true}},"title":"resources\examples\gummy-bears\llm-calls\actions-20261113T140800-b0a1\prompt.txt","time":{"start":1794575307092,"end":1794575307143}},"id":"prt_1d5061030001NJIGZQowbyhFA3","sessionID":"ses_e2afa4596ffeNNoPkxEueF6bCf","messageID":"msg_1d505f68e001LARVF4LDW4rLQ3"}}

1: #!/usr/bin/env python3
2: """
3: gummibear_analyses.py -- Session B analysis pipeline, gummy bear paper.
4: 
5: Runs all main analyses end to end from the three analysis-ready CSVs built in
6: session A (documented in data/codebook.md) and writes analysis/results_2026-08-17.md
7: as a numbered results log. Every number that could end up in the paper appears
8: there together with the analysis that produced it.
9: 
10: Reproduce, from the project root:
11:     python3 analysis/gummibear_analyses.py
12: Optionally run the R control analyses afterwards and re-run this script; the log
13: then includes the R-vs-Python comparison in section 9:
14:     bash analysis/setup-r-sandbox.sh   (once per sandbox session, ~8 min)
15:     MAMBA_ROOT_PREFIX=/tmp/mamba /tmp/bin/micromamba run -n renv Rscript analysis/control_analyses.R
16:     python3 analysis/gummibear_analyses.py
17: 
18: Inference conventions (PROJECT.md pinned decision, 2026-08-17):
19:   - Primary inference: permutation tests, exact binomial tests and intervals,
20:     and trial-level bootstrap. Mixed models are R-side control analyses only.
21:   - Permutation p = (1 + #{|T_perm| >= |T_obs|}) / (N_PERM + 1), two-sided,
22:     except AUC tests, which are one-sided upper (H1: discrimination above
23:     chance), marked "one-sided" where reported.
24:   - Exact enumeration where the permutation space is small (n = 4 persons:
25:     4! = 24 orderings; n = 6 flavors: 6! = 720 orderings); p is then the exact
26:     proportion of |r_perm| >= |r_obs|, identity included, and the smallest
27:     attainable p is 1/24 = .042 resp. 1/720 = .0014.
28:   - Confidence intervals for proportions: Clopper-Pearson exact, 95%.
29:   - Exploratory study: exact p-values reported, no multiplicity correction.
30:   - 4 perceivers cannot support inferential variance estimation or a
31:     perceiver-level bootstrap; where that bites, the log says so instead of
32:     reporting a fragile interval.
33: 
34: Inputs (never the source workbook):
35:     data/gummibear_trials.csv        100 trials, derived columns per codebook
36:     data/gummibear_apriori.csv       4 persons, per-flavor a priori measures
37:     data/gummibear_apriori_long.csv  24 person x flavor cells
38: Outputs:
39:     analysis/results_2026-08-17.md   numbered results log
40:     analysis/py_auc_by_cell.csv      24 cell AUCs, input to the R comparison
41: 
42: Fixed seed; single rng consumed in fixed program order, so the log reproduces
43: byte-identically. Runtime approx. 1-2 minutes.
44: """
45: 
46: from __future__ import annotations
47: 
48: import itertools
49: import math
50: import platform
51: from pathlib import Path
52: 
53: import numpy as np
54: import pandas as pd
55: import scipy
56: from scipy import stats
57: 
58: # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
59: # Constants
60: # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
61: SEED = 20240805          # date of session 1 of data collection
62: N_PERM = 10_000
63: N_BOOT = 10_000
64: N_SIM = 10_000           # noise-floor simulations, variance decomposition
65: RESULTS_DATE = "2026-08-17"
66: CHANCE = 1.0 / 6.0
67: 
68: ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
69: DATA = ROOT / "data"
70: OUT = ROOT / "analysis"
71: 
72: FLAVORS = ["E", "O", "Ap", "H", "Z", "An"]
73: FLAVORS_EN = {"E": "strawberry", "O": "orange", "Ap": "apple",
74:               "H": "raspberry", "Z": "lemon", "An": "pineapple"}
75: PERSONS = ["Ada", "Ella", "Natalie", "Mitja"]  # person_id order 1..4
76: 
77: rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
78: L: list[str] = []        # the results log, one string per line
79: 
80: 
81: # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
82: # Small helpers
83: # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
84: def w(line: str = "") -> None:
85:     L.append(line)
86: 
87: 
88: def fmt(x: float, d: int = 3) -> str:
89:     return f"{x:.{d}f}"
90: 
91: 
92: def fmtp(p: float) -> str:
93:     # Reporting floor, PROJECT.md pin 2026-08-29: with 10,000 draws and the
94:     # (1 + count) / (B + 1) correction the smallest attainable permutation p is
95:     # 1/10001, so anything at or near that resolution limit is reported as
96:     # "< .001" rather than "< .0001". The four-decimal branch is unchanged, so
97:     # exactly computed values such as p = .0056 keep their own precision.
98:     return "< .001" if p < 1e-4 else f"= {p:.4f}"
99: 
100: 
101: def binom_ci(k: int, n: int) -> tuple[float, float]:
102:     ci = stats.binomtest(k, n).proportion_ci(confidence_level=0.95, method="exact")
103:     return ci.low, ci.high
104: 
105: 
106: def binom_p(k: int, n: int, p0: float) -> float:
107:     return stats.binomtest(k, n, p0).pvalue  # two-sided (minlike)
108: 
109: 
110: def ffh_exact(counts: np.ndarray, n_each: int) -> tuple[float, float, int]:
111:     """Exact conditional test of homogeneity for a k x 2 table with equal row
112:     totals (Fisher-Freeman-Halton by enumeration). Returns
113:     (chi-square of the observed table, exact p, number of tables enumerated).
114:     Deterministic: no rng consumed."""
115:     def chi2_of(h: list[int] | np.ndarray) -> float:
116:         obs = np.array([[x, n_each - x] for x in h], dtype=float)
117:         exp = np.outer(obs.sum(1), obs.sum(0)) / obs.sum()
118:         return float(((obs - exp) ** 2 / exp).sum())
119: 
120:     def logC(a: int, b: int) -> float:
121:         return (math.lgamma(a + 1) - math.lgamma(b + 1)
122:                 - math.lgamma(a - b + 1))
123: 
124:     counts = [int(c) for c in counts]
125:     k, tot = len(counts), sum(counts)
126:     obs_chi = chi2_of(counts)
127:     den = logC(k * n_each, tot)
128:     p, n_tab = 0.0, 0
129:     for h in itertools.product(range(n_each + 1), repeat=k - 1):
130:         last = tot - sum(h)
131:         if not 0 <= last <= n_each:
132:             continue
133:         tabl = list(h) + [last]
134:         n_tab += 1
135:         pr = math.exp(sum(logC(n_each, x) for x in tabl) - den)
136:         if chi2_of(tabl) >= obs_chi - 1e-9:
137:             p += pr
138:     return obs_chi, float(p), n_tab
139:

141: def dc(M: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
142:     """Double-center: cell - row mean - column mean + grand mean."""
143:     return M - M.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True) - M.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True) + M.mean()
144: 
145: 
146: def pearson(x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> float:
147:     return float(np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1])
148: 
149: 
150: def wpearson(x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, wt: np.ndarray) -> float:
151:     xm = np.average(x, weights=wt)
152:     ym = np.average(y, weights=wt)
153:     cov = np.average((x - xm) * (y - ym), weights=wt)
154:     vx = np.average((x - xm) ** 2, weights=wt)
155:     vy = np.average((y - ym) ** 2, weights=wt)
156:     return float(cov / np.sqrt(vx * vy))
157: 
158: 
159: def exact_perm_r(x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> tuple[float, float, int]:
160:     """Exact permutation test for a correlation with tiny n: enumerate all
161:     orderings of y. Returns (r_obs, exact two-sided p, n_perms)."""
162:     r_obs = pearson(x, y)
163:     perms = list(itertools.permutations(range(len(y))))
164:     rs = np.array([pearson(x, y[list(p)]) for p in perms])
165:     p = float(np.mean(np.abs(rs) >= abs(r_obs) - 1e-12))
166:     return r_obs, p, len(perms)
167: 
168: 
169: def perm_p_two(obs: float, null: np.ndarray) -> float:
170:     return float((1 + np.sum(np.abs(null) >= abs(obs) - 1e-12)) / (len(null) + 1))
171: 
172: 
173: def perm_p_upper(obs: float, null: np.ndarray) -> float:
174:     return float((1 + np.sum(null >= obs - 1e-12)) / (len(null) + 1))
175: 
176: 
177: def auc_from_ranks(rank_sum_pos: float, n1: int, n0: int) -> float:
178:     return (rank_sum_pos - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2.0) / (n1 * n0)
179: 
180: 
181: def auc_mw(pos: np.ndarray, neg: np.ndarray) -> float:
182:     """Mann-Whitney AUC with midranks (ties handled)."""
183:     allv = np.concatenate([pos, neg])
184:     ranks = stats.rankdata(allv)
185:     return auc_from_ranks(float(ranks[: len(pos)].sum()), len(pos), len(neg))

631: def stratified_trend(y_col: str, x_col: str, cells: list[np.ndarray],
632:                      ydata: np.ndarray, xdata: np.ndarray,
633:                      n_perm: int) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
634:     """Permutation trend test of y on x, stratified by person x flavor cell.
635:     Within each cell, x is centered; T = sum over trials of xc * y. Null:
636:     y shuffled within cell. Returns (T_obs, r_strat, p_two)."""
637:     xc = np.concatenate([xdata[idx] - xdata[idx].mean() for idx in cells])
638:     yv = np.concatenate([ydata[idx] for idx in cells])
639:     ycent = np.concatenate([ydata[idx] - ydata[idx].mean() for idx in cells])
640:     T_obs = float(xc @ yv)
641:     denom = np.sqrt((xc ** 2).sum() * (ycent ** 2).sum())
642:     r_strat = T_obs / denom if denom > 0 else np.nan
643:     sizes = [len(idx) for idx in cells]
644:     null = np.empty(n_perm)
645:     for it in range(n_perm):
646:         parts = []
647:         pos = 0
648:         for idx, s in zip(cells, sizes):
649:             parts.append(rng.permutation(ydata[idx]))
650:             pos += s
651:         null[it] = xc @ np.concatenate(parts)
652:     return T_obs, float(r_strat), perm_p_two(T_obs, null)

961: def rel_effects_weighted_tasted() -> np.ndarray:
962:     """Relationship effects for tasted liking with trial-based (weighted)
963:     margins: cell mean - person trial mean - flavor trial mean + grand trial
964:     mean."""
965:     pmean = trials.groupby("person")["liking"].mean().reindex(PERSONS).to_numpy()
966:     fmean = trials.groupby("true_flavor")["liking"].mean().reindex(FLAVORS).to_numpy()
967:     grand = trials["liking"].mean()
968:     return M_tlike - pmean[:, None] - fmean[None, :] + grand

    chance), marked "one-sided" where reported.

    4! = 24 orderings; n = 6 flavors: 6! = 720 orderings); p is then the exact
    proportion of |r_perm| >= |r_obs|, identity included, and the smallest
    attainable p is 1/24 = .042 resp. 1/720 = .0014.
  - Confidence intervals for proportions: Clopper-Pearson exact, 95%.

    reporting a fragile interval.

    data/gummibear_trials.csv        100 trials, derived columns per codebook

byte-identically. Runtime approx. 1-2 minutes.

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import math
import platform
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import scipy
from scipy import stats

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Constants
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

N_PERM = 10_000
N_BOOT = 10_000
N_SIM = 10_000           # noise-floor simulations, variance decomposition
RESULTS_DATE = "2026-08-17"
CHANCE = 1.0 / 6.0

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
DATA = ROOT / "data"
OUT = ROOT / "analysis"

FLAVORS = ["E", "O", "Ap", "H", "Z", "An"]

              "H": "raspberry", "Z": "lemon", "An": "pineapple"}

L: list[str] = []        # the results log, one string per line


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Small helpers
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def w(line: str = "") -> None:

def fmt(x: float, d: int = 3) -> str:
    return f"{x:.{d}f}"


def fmtp(p: float) -> str:
    # Reporting floor, PROJECT.md pin 2026-08-29: with 10,000 draws and the
    # (1 + count) / (B + 1) correction the smallest attainable permutation p is
    # 1/10001, so anything at or near that resolution limit is reported as
    # "< .001" rather than "< .0001". The four-decimal branch is unchanged, so
    # exactly computed values such as p = .0056 keep their own precision.
    return "< .001" if p < 1e-4 else f"= {p:.4f}"


def binom_ci(k: int, n: int) -> tuple[float, float]:
    ci = stats.binomtest(k, n).proportion_ci(confidence_level=0.95, method="exact")
    return ci.low, ci.high


def binom_p(k: int, n: int, p0: float) -> float:
    return stats.binomtest(k, n, p0).pvalue  # two-sided (minlike)


def ffh_exact(counts: np.ndarray, n_each: int) -> tuple[float, float, int]:
    """Exact conditional test of homogeneity for a k x 2 table with equal row
    totals (Fisher-Freeman-Halton by enumeration). Returns
    (chi-square of the observed table, exact p, number of tables enumerated).
    Deterministic: no rng consumed."""
    def chi2_of(h: list[int] | np.ndarray) -> float:
        obs = np.array([[x, n_each - x] for x in h], dtype=float)
        exp = np.outer(obs.sum(1), obs.sum(0)) / obs.sum()
        return float(((obs - exp) ** 2 / exp).sum())

    def logC(a: int, b: int) -> float:
        return (math.lgamma(a + 1) - math.lgamma(b + 1)
                - math.lgamma(a - b + 1))

    counts = [int(c) for c in counts]
    k, tot = len(counts), sum(counts)
    obs_chi = chi2_of(counts)
    den = logC(k * n_each, tot)
    p, n_tab = 0.0, 0
    for h in itertools.product(range(n_each + 1), repeat=k - 1):
        last = tot - sum(h)
        if not 0 <= last <= n_each:
            continue
        tabl = list(h) + [last]
        n_tab += 1
        pr = math.exp(sum(logC(n_each, x) for x in tabl) - den)
        if chi2_of(tabl) >= obs_chi - 1e-9:
            p += pr
    return obs_chi, float(p), n_tab


def dc(M: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Double-center: cell - row mean - column mean + grand mean."""
    return M - M.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True) - M.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True) + M.mean()


def pearson(x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> float:
    return float(np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1])


def wpearson(x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, wt: np.ndarray) -> float:
    xm = np.average(x, weights=wt)
    ym = np.average(y, weights=wt)
    cov = np.average((x - xm) * (y - ym), weights=wt)
    vx = np.average((x - xm) ** 2, weights=wt)
    vy = np.average((y - ym) ** 2, weights=wt)
    return float(cov / np.sqrt(vx * vy))


def exact_perm_r(x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> tuple[float, float, int]:
    """Exact permutation test for a correlation with tiny n: enumerate all
    orderings of y. Returns (r_obs, exact two-sided p, n_perms)."""
    r_obs = pearson(x, y)
    perms = list(itertools.permutations(range(len(y))))
    rs = np.array([pearson(x, y[list(p)]) for p in perms])
    p = float(np.mean(np.abs(rs) >= abs(r_obs) - 1e-12))
    return r_obs, p, len(perms)


def perm_p_two(obs: float, null: np.ndarray) -> float:
    return float((1 + np.sum(np.abs(null) >= abs(obs) - 1e-12)) / (len(null) + 1))


def perm_p_upper(obs: float, null: np.ndarray) -> float:
    return float((1 + np.sum(null >= obs - 1e-12)) / (len(null) + 1))


def auc_from_ranks(rank_sum_pos: float, n1: int, n0: int) -> float:
    return (rank_sum_pos - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2.0) / (n1 * n0)

    """Mann-Whitney AUC with midranks (ties handled)."""
    allv = np.concatenate([pos, neg])
    ranks = stats.rankdata(allv)
    return auc_from_ranks(float(ranks[: len(pos)].sum()), len(pos), len(neg))
